1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, bounded
10	  `loop`, and dynamic `map` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- a map node inside a loop body expands independently in every iteration
30	  from that iteration's source output, its instances and events belonging
31	  to the iteration they expanded in;
32	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
33	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
34	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
35	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
36	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
37	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
38	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
39	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
40	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
41	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
42	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
43	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
44	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
45	- subscriptions may also declare queue targets instead of webhook addresses:
46	  matching business events are appended, in occurrence order, to persistent
47	  per-execution queues that callers pull from and acknowledge explicitly,
48	  with a visibility timeout returning unacknowledged messages to the pending
49	  set (delivery is at least once);
50	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
51	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
52	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
53	  resumed, periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
54	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy, and a read-only preview
55	  query projects the upcoming trigger times and their inputs.
56	
57	## Requirements
58	
59	- Python 3.11 or newer
60	- no third-party runtime dependencies
61	
62	## Run the service
63	
64	```bash
65	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
66	```
67	
68	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
69	has bound the port.
70	
71	## HTTP API
72	
73	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
74	
75	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
76	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
77	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
78	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
79	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
80	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
81	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
82	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
83	
84	### Tenants and quotas
85	
86	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
87	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
88	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
89	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
90	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
91	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
92	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
93	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
94	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
95	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
96	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
97	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
98	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
99	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
100	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
101	
102	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
103	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
104	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, instance deletion and
105	modification and re-expansion, queue pulls, acknowledgements, and all
106	history and status queries, as well as the quota declaration, the price
107	declaration and price delete, the price read and the price change history, and the usage, bill, and
108	metrics queries. An empty
109	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
110	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
111	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
112	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
113	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
114	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
115	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
116	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
117	the usual `409 conflict`.
118	
119	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
120	hold:
121	
122	```http
123	PUT /quotas
124	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
125	X-Tenant-Id: acme
126	
127	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
128	```
129	
130	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
131	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
132	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
133	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
134	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
135	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
136	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
137	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
138	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
139	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
140	
141	```http
142	GET /quotas
143	X-Tenant-Id: acme
144	```
145	
146	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
147	when the tenant has declared none.
148	
149	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
150	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
151	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
152	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
153	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
154	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
155	
156	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
157	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
158	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
159	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
160	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
161	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
162	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
163	
164	### Tenant price tables
165	
166	The bill's baseline unit prices are built in. A tenant may instead declare
167	its own price table on a separate entry point with the same calling shape as
168	the quota declaration:
169	
170	```http
171	PUT /prices
172	Idempotency-Key: price-request-1
173	X-Tenant-Id: acme
174	
175	{"execution_started":200,"workflow_created":1500}
176	```
177	
178	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must be a non-empty
179	JSON object giving a map of metered action type to a positive-integer unit
180	price in cents. A non-positive, non-integer, boolean, or non-finite price,
181	an unknown metered type, a missing field (an empty object), an extra field
182	that is not a metered type, or a non-object body is a `400
183	validation_error` that writes nothing. Every price route requires a tenant:
184	declaring, deleting, and reading without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
185	one) is a `400 validation_error`, and an unknown query parameter on the
186	read or the delete is rejected the same way, with the message naming the
187	offending parameter. The response is
188	`{"prices":{"execution_started":200,"workflow_created":1500}}`, with the
189	declared types in ascending type-identifier order.
190	
191	A successful declaration replaces the tenant's price table as a whole with
192	exactly the types given this time; metered types the declaration does not
193	name fall back to the built-in default prices when a bill is taken. The
194	declaration rewrites no recorded usage counts and changes no bill taken
195	before it was made.
196	
197	```http
198	GET /prices
199	X-Tenant-Id: acme
200	```
201	
202	Returns the price table currently declared by the tenant, in ascending
203	type-identifier order, or the definite empty result `{"prices":null}` for a
204	tenant that has never declared one. The stored table lists only the types
205	the declaration named; types left at the default are not copied into it.
206	
207	A tenant can also remove the table it declared, on the same path with the
208	`DELETE` method and the same calling shape as the other price writes:
209	
210	```http
211	DELETE /prices
212	Idempotency-Key: price-delete-1
213	X-Tenant-Id: acme
214	
215	{}
216	```
217	
218	The body must be exactly an empty object; a non-empty or non-object body,
219	an unknown field, or a non-finite value is a `400 validation_error` that
220	touches no price table. The delete removes the table as a whole and leaves
221	no partial write: it is atomic with the declaration and the read, so a
222	concurrent reader sees either the complete old table or no table at all.
223	After it succeeds the tenant no longer holds a declared table, and both the
224	delete response and the following read give the definite empty result
225	`{"prices":null}`. Deleting the table of a tenant that never declared one
226	returns that same definite empty result rather than an error. The delete
227	rewrites no recorded usage counts and changes no bill taken before it was
228	made; afterward both the bill and the bucketed bill price every type at the
229	built-in default, each line still giving the metered type, the actual
230	`unit_price` used, the `count`, and the integer-cent `subtotal`.
231	
232	The declaration and the delete follow the same idempotency rules as every
233	other write: the `Idempotency-Key` header is required, repeating the same
234	declaration or the same delete with the same key returns the first result
235	and performs no second replacement or removal, and reusing a key for
236	another operation — including another price declaration or a price delete
237	— in the same tenant is a `409 conflict` that leaves the tenant's price
238	table unchanged. Price tables are scoped per tenant like everything else: a
239	tenant can never read or delete another's declaration, and another tenant's
240	declaration or deletion never affects this tenant's bill amounts.
241	
242	The bill and the bucketed bill price with the price table in effect **at
243	query time**: a named type uses the tenant's declared price and every other
244	type uses the built-in default. Each returned line still gives the metered
245	type, the actual `unit_price` used, the `count`, and the integer-cent
246	`subtotal`, and the total is exactly the sum of the listed subtotals; types
247	with no matching record are still omitted rather than listed at zero. A
248	declaration affects only later queries — it neither rewrites recorded usage
249	nor revises historical bills — changes no metering, and leaves the bill and
250	usage queries read-only. A delete affects only later queries in the same
251	way: the table is removed as a whole, later bills fall back to the
252	built-in defaults, and recorded usage and already-taken bills stay exactly
253	as they were.
254	
255	### Price-table change history
256	
257	Every successful price-table declaration or delete leaves one change record,
258	so a caller can see exactly when each repricing and each table removal took
259	effect. A separate entry point returns the tenant's change history:
260	
261	```http
262	GET /prices/history?limit=50
263	X-Tenant-Id: acme
264	```
265	
266	Returns `{"history":[...]}` with the records in ascending order of occurrence
267	time; records sharing one instant are ordered by a stable ascending sequence.
268	Each record is:
269	
270	```json
271	{"sequence":7,"action":"declare","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z","snapshot":{"execution_started":200}}
272	```
273	
274	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant,
275	  shared across every kind of price change. It identifies the record across
276	  every query and is never renumbered by a filter or a page;
277	- `action` is `declare` for a price-table declaration or `delete` for a
278	  removal;
279	- `occurred_at` is the moment the change took effect, an ISO-8601 UTC string
280	  ending in `Z`;
281	- `snapshot` is the table in effect after the change. A declaration's
282	  snapshot is the type-to-unit-price map that took effect, listing only the
283	  types that declaration named and in ascending type-identifier order; a
284	  delete's snapshot is `null`.
285	
286	The history record is written atomically with the change it describes, in the
287	same transaction as the price-table write, so a reader always sees the table
288	and its history agree and a rejected declaration, delete, or idempotency-key
289	conflict leaves no record. Repeating an idempotent declaration or delete with
290	the same key returns the first result and appends no second record; reusing a
291	key for another operation is the usual `409 conflict` and, again, writes no
292	history. A delete of a table that was never declared still succeeds and still
293	leaves its own `delete` record (with a `null` snapshot), exactly as it returns
294	the definite empty result for the table itself.
295	
296	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
297	`{"history":[]}`, never an error. The response is one line of compact JSON
298	with the record keys in the order above, full number precision preserved, and
299	a single trailing newline, like every other JSON endpoint.
300	
301	The endpoint accepts an optional action filter, the same optional closed time
302	window the per-record usage query accepts, plus cursor pagination:
303	
304	```http
305	GET /prices/history?action=declare,delete&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
306	```
307	
308	- `action` names one action or a comma-separated set of them (`declare` and
309	  `delete`); only records whose action is in the set are returned. A single
310	  value needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown
311	  action is a `400 validation_error`; when `action` is absent every change is
312	  returned;
313	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
314	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
315	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
316	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches nothing
317	  and the definite empty list is returned;
318	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
319	  contains more than that many records;
320	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
321	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
322	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
323	- the action filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
324	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
325	
326	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `action` entry, a
327	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
328	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
329	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
330	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. The query is read-only: it
331	appends no history, changes no price table, and changes no metering, usage,
332	bill, quota, or scheduling conclusion. History follows the usual tenant
333	isolation, so another tenant's changes are never visible under any action
334	filter, window, or page and never affect this tenant's result; replay and
335	recovery leave every recorded sequence, time, and snapshot unchanged.
336	
337	### Usage metering and billing
338	
339	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
340	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
341	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
342	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
343	metered action types are:
344	
345	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
346	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
347	  definition;
348	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
349	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
350	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
351	  `schedule_triggered`;
352	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
353	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
354	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
355	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
356	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
357	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
358	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
359	  meters nothing.
360	
361	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
362	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
363	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
364	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
365	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
366	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
367	
368	```http
369	GET /usage
370	X-Tenant-Id: acme
371	```
372	
373	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
374	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
375	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
376	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
377	
378	```http
379	GET /bill
380	X-Tenant-Id: acme
381	```
382	
383	Returns the per-type bill:
384	
385	```json
386	{"bill":{"items":[
387	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
388	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
389	],"total":2100}}
390	```
391	
392	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
393	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
394	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
395	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`. The price used per type is
396	the tenant's declared price when its price table names that type and the
397	built-in default otherwise, read from the table in effect at query time (see
398	[Tenant price tables](#tenant-price-tables)); tenants with no declaration are
399	billed byte for byte as before.
400	
401	Both endpoints accept the same optional query parameters the events and
402	metrics queries accept: an optional metered-type filter and an ISO-8601 UTC
403	timestamp window, each timestamp ending in `Z`, plus an optional fixed time
404	bucket:
405	
406	```http
407	GET /usage?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
408	GET /bill?type=execution_started&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
409	X-Tenant-Id: acme
410	```
411	
412	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them; only
413	  records whose type is in the set are counted. A single identifier needs no
414	  comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered type is a
415	  `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is counted, exactly
416	  as before;
417	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on each usage record's
418	  occurrence time: a record whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted.
419	  When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting
420	  both returns exactly the cumulative result above;
421	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
422	  parameter is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing;
423	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
424	  simply contains no records. Usage then reports the definite empty result
425	  `{"usage":[]}`, and the bill reports an empty `items` list with a `total` of
426	  `0`.
427	
428	The type filter and the time window apply together as an intersection: a
429	record is counted only when its type is named **and** its occurrence time is
430	in the window. A type the filter names but that has no matching record is
431	omitted rather than reported at zero, so a filter that matches nothing gives
432	the same definite empty results as an empty window: `{"usage":[]}` for usage
433	and an empty `items` list with a `total` of `0` for the bill.
434	
435	Both endpoints also accept an optional `bucket` parameter for a fixed-bucket
436	trend summary, so callers never have to pull records and group them
437	themselves:
438	
439	```http
440	GET /usage?bucket=hour&since=2026-09-26T00:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-27T00:00:00.000Z
441	GET /bill?bucket=day&type=execution_started
442	X-Tenant-Id: acme
443	```
444	
445	- `bucket` is exactly `hour` or `day`: `hour` buckets start on the UTC hour
446	  and `day` buckets at UTC midnight, both aligned solely to UTC. An empty or
447	  any other value is a `400 validation_error`, exactly like a repeated
448	  parameter or an unknown query parameter;
449	- when `bucket` is present, usage returns
450	  `{"usage_buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T08:00:00Z","usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}, ...]}`:
451	  the buckets with at least one matching record, in ascending bucket-start
452	  order. Each entry gives its `bucket_start` first — an ISO-8601 UTC string
453	  ending in `Z` at the hour or midnight — followed by `usage`, the per-type
454	  counts inside that bucket in ascending type-identifier order; a type with no
455	  record in the bucket is omitted;
456	- when `bucket` is present, the bill returns
457	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T00:00:00Z","items":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100}, ...],"subtotal":100}, ...],"total":100}}`.
458	  Buckets appear in ascending bucket-start order; each bucket's `items` stay
459	  sorted by ascending type identifier, each line giving the filtered count,
460	  the usual positive-integer `unit_price`, and an integer-cent `subtotal` of
461	  the two, and a type with no matching record is omitted rather than reported
462	  at zero. Each bucket also carries its own `subtotal`, and the window
463	  `total` is exactly the sum of the listed per-bucket subtotals, all amounts
464	  integer cents;
465	- a bucket that holds no matching record never appears, so an empty tenant, a
466	  window with `since` later than `until`, or a filter that matches nothing
467	  returns the definite empty bucket lists `{"usage_buckets":[]}` and
468	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[],"total":0}` — never an error, with the empty bill's
469	  total at `0`;
470	- bucketing applies together with the type filter and the time window as an
471	  intersection: a bucket holds only records whose occurrence time is in the
472	  closed window **and** whose type the filter names. The window keeps its
473	  closed endpoints, its open bounds when either side is omitted, and the
474	  existing rule for when a record's instant falls in it; buckets are simply
475	  the same matching records rolled up to their UTC bucket;
476	- the bucketed queries are read-only like the others: they append no usage
477	  records, change no metering basis or prices, and never alter recorded usage
478	  or billing conclusions — under event replay or recovery the same window,
479	  type filter, and bucket always give the same answer;
480	- omitting `bucket` leaves both queries exactly as before: the same compact
481	  JSON responses with `usage` / `items` shapes, full float precision and the
482	  `-0.0` convention, byte for byte. The parameter introduces no second
483	  protocol and changes no entry point's existing behavior.
484	
485	Only records whose occurrence time falls in the window are counted. Within
486	the window the bill keeps the same basis as always: each present type reports
487	its filtered, windowed count, its usual `unit_price`, and a `subtotal` of the
488	two; items stay sorted by ascending type identifier, and a type with no
489	matching record is omitted rather than reported at zero. The bill's `total`
490	is exactly the sum of the subtotals of the listed items. The query is
491	read-only: it writes no usage records, changes no prices or metering
492	conclusions, and never alters already recorded usage — under event replay or
493	recovery the same window and type filter always give the same answer.
494	
495	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
496	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error` that reveals no usage. Usage and
497	bill data follow the usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see
498	another's records under any type filter or window, and another tenant's
499	records never affect this tenant's counts or totals.
500	
501	### Per-record usage history
502	
503	The cumulative usage query reports only per-type totals. A separate endpoint
504	returns the individual usage records themselves, so each billed action can be
505	checked against the moment it occurred:
506	
507	```http
508	GET /usage/records?limit=50
509	X-Tenant-Id: acme
510	```
511	
512	Returns `{"records":[...]}` with the matching records in ascending order of
513	occurrence time; records sharing one instant are ordered by ascending
514	sequence. Each record is:
515	
516	```json
517	{"sequence":7,"type":"execution_started","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z"}
518	```
519	
520	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant. It
521	  identifies the record across every query and is never renumbered by a
522	  filter or a page;
523	- `type` is the metered action type;
524	- `occurred_at` is the record's occurrence time as an ISO-8601 UTC string
525	  ending in `Z`.
526	
527	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
528	`{"records":[]}`, never an error. The response ends with a single newline,
529	like every other JSON endpoint.
530	
531	The endpoint accepts an optional metered-type filter, the same optional
532	closed time window the events and usage queries accept, plus cursor
533	pagination:
534	
535	```http
536	GET /usage/records?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
537	```
538	
539	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them;
540	  only records whose type is in the set are returned. A single identifier
541	  needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered
542	  type is a `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is
543	  returned, exactly as before;
544	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
545	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
546	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
547	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches
548	  nothing and the definite empty list is returned;
549	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
550	  contains more than that many records;
551	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
552	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
553	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
554	- the type filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
555	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
556	
557	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `type` entry, a
558	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
559	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
560	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
561	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. The query is read-only: it
562	appends no usage records, writes no events, and changes no metering, prices,
563	quotas, or billing conclusions. Records follow the usual tenant isolation, so
564	another tenant's records are never visible under any type filter, window, or
565	page and never affect this tenant's result; replay and recovery leave every
566	recorded sequence, time, and billing conclusion unchanged.
567	
568	### Operational metrics
569	
570	```http
571	GET /metrics
572	X-Tenant-Id: acme
573	```
574	
575	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
576	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
577	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
578	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
579	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
580	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
581	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
582	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
583	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
584	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
585	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
586	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
587	
588	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
589	timestamp ending in `Z`:
590	
591	```http
592	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
593	X-Tenant-Id: acme
594	```
595	
596	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
597	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
598	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
599	  counts every recorded fact;
600	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
601	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
602	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
603	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
604	  result.
605	
606	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
607	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
608	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
609	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
610	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
611	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
612	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
613	completion or termination event.
614	
615	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
616	
617	```http
618	GET /metrics/export
619	X-Tenant-Id: acme
620	```
621	
622	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
623	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
624	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
625	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
626	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
627	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
628	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
629	
630	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
631	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
632	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
633	ordered by ascending label value:
634	
635	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
636	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
637	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
638	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
639	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
640	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
641	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
642	  unlabeled scalar samples.
643	
644	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
645	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
646	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
647	ends with a single newline.
648	
649	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
650	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
651	failures, and schedule triggers:
652	
653	```json
654	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
655	```
656	
657	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
658	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
659	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
660	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
661	  ended for that reason.
662	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
663	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
664	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
665	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
666	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
667	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
668	  another attempt, per node identifier.
669	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
670	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
671	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
672	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
673	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
674	
675	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
676	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
677	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
678	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
679	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
680	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.
681	
682	### Health
683	
684	```http
685	GET /health
686	```
687	
688	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
689	
690	### Create a workflow
691	
692	```http
693	POST /workflows
694	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
695	
696	{
697	  "id": "order-flow",
698	  "nodes": [
699	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
700	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
701	  ]
702	}
703	```
704	
705	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
706	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
707	
708	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
709	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
710	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
711	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
712	
713	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
714	
715	```json
716	{
717	  "id": "order-flow",
718	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
719	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
720	}
721	```
722	
723	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
724	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
725	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
726	
727	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
728	
729	```json
730	{
731	  "id": "nightly-orders",
732	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
733	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
734	}
735	```
736	
737	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
738	
739	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
740	
741	```json
742	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
743	```
744	
745	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
746	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
747	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
748	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
749	`false`.
750	
751	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
752	
753	```json
754	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
755	```
756	
757	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
758	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
759	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
760	dependencies of its successors.
761	
762	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
763	
764	```json
765	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
766	```
767	
768	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
769	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
770	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
771	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
772	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
773	`retries_exhausted`.
774	
775	A task may instead declare an approval point:
776	
777	```json
778	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
779	```
780	
781	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
782	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
783	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
784	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
785	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
786	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
787	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
788	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
789	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
790	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
791	move the task.
792	
793	### Submit an approval decision
794	
795	```http
796	POST /executions/run-1/decision
797	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
798	
799	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
800	```
801	
802	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
803	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
804	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
805	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
806	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
807	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
808	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
809	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
810	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
811	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
812	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
813	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
814	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
815	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
816	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
817	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
818	404.
819	
820	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
821	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
822	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
823	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
824	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
825	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
826	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
827	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
828	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
829	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
830	shape and event stream.
831	
832	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
833	segment:
834	
835	```json
836	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
837	```
838	
839	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
840	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
841	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
842	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
843	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
844	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
845	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
846	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
847	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
848	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
849	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
850	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
851	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
852	loop node instead).
853	
854	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
855	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
856	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
857	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
858	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
859	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
860	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
861	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
862	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
863	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
864	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
865	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
866	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
867	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
868	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
869	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
870	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
871	belong only to their iterations.
872	
873	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
874	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
875	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
876	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
877	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
878	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
879	exactly.
880	
881	### Dynamic map nodes
882	
883	A `map` node expands at runtime into one task instance per element of a
884	recorded array:
885	
886	```json
887	{"id": "ship", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["collect"],
888	 "source": "collect", "path": "items", "max_instances": 100,
889	 "template": {"id": "ship-item", "retries": 2}}
890	```
891	
892	A map node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `source`, `path`,
893	`max_instances`, and `template`; any other field is rejected as unknown.
894	
895	- `source` names a `task` node that is also listed in `depends_on`. Expansion
896	  begins only after every dependency has completed or been skipped; the
897	  element list comes solely from the source task's recorded output.
898	- `path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into that recorded output, using
899	  the same path syntax as a condition.
900	- `max_instances` is a positive integer bounding how many elements may
901	  expand.
902	- `template` describes the single task each instance runs and contains
903	  exactly an `id`, and optionally `retries` (an integer between 0 and 10,
904	  defaulting to 0) and an `approval` point with the same shape a task node
905	  uses. The template id only names the dynamically expanded instances; it
906	  may coincide with a declared node id or with another map's template id.
907	  A map node may also sit inside a loop body, expanding independently in
908	  every iteration (see "Maps inside loop bodies" below).
909	
910	When the dependencies settle, the value at `path` is read once. When it is an
911	array, one instance is created per element; the instances queue in ascending
912	element index order. Each `advance` still settles exactly one ready item, so
913	instances are worked in index order, one per call. An instance is an ordinary
914	task in every other respect: a submitted failure consumes the template's
915	retry bound and re-queues that instance, and a template approval point parks
916	the execution with the instance's `map_id` and `index` recorded, until an
917	approver decides it. Retries and approvals are per instance: results never
918	overwrite another instance.
919	
920	When every instance is completed, the map node completes and its output,
921	recorded both in the node's `outputs` entry and under its `maps` record, is
922	the list of instance outputs in ascending element order; its successors then
923	become available in the usual way.
924	
925	A value that is missing or is not an array expands to zero instances: the map
926	completes with an empty output list and releases its successors immediately.
927	When the array holds more elements than `max_instances`, no instance is
928	created at all: the map node fails permanently, is listed under
929	`failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`
930	under the usual exhaustion semantics.
931	
932	Execution state exposes each map under `maps`: the node's `status`
933	(`pending`, `running`, `completed`, or `failed`), one record per retained
934	instance giving its `index`, `status` (`ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, or
935	`failed`), its `output`, and its `failure_reason` (null except for a
936	permanently failed instance), plus the ordered completed `outputs` list and
937	the node's single `failure_reason`. A `ready` instance that has been
938	rewritten by a successful modify additionally carries that rewritten
939	`input`; every other instance record keeps exactly these fields. The `maps`
940	field is present only when the bound workflow declares a map node outside
941	any loop body; every other execution keeps its previous state shape.
942	
943	The event stream records a `map_expanded` event when expansion happens,
944	carrying the map id and the number of created instances (zero for a missing
945	or non-array value, and zero together with `exceeded` and the observed
946	element count when the bound is exceeded), and a `map_completed` event with
947	the map id and final instance count. Each instance's per-node events —
948	`node_completed`, `node_failed`, and `node_retried`, plus
949	`approval_requested` and `approval_decided` for a template approval point —
950	carry their `map_id` and element `index` alongside the template node id, so
951	replay rebuilds every instance solely from the event stream. Checkpoints are
952	written at instance boundaries, so recovery resumes with the unfinished
953	instances and never repeats an instance output. Per-instance completions and
954	failures count toward the existing node metrics under the template node id,
955	and webhook and queue subscriptions receive instance events exactly like any
956	other node event. Instance deletion and modification add their own
957	`instance_deleted` and `instance_modified` events, and re-expansion adds a
958	`map_reexpanded` event, described under
959	"Delete and modify expanded instances" below.
960	
961	### Maps inside loop bodies
962	
963	A map node may belong to a loop body — it is part of the body exactly when
964	the loop's entry or condition reaches it through `depends_on`, like any
965	other body member:
966	
967	```json
968	{"id": "fanout", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["attempt"],
969	 "source": "attempt", "path": "items", "max_instances": 10,
970	 "template": {"id": "work", "retries": 1}}
971	```
972	
973	A nested map expands once per iteration, when every dependency of its node
974	is completed or skipped in that iteration, and the element list is read from
975	the source task's output of that same iteration. The expansion rules are the
976	ones of an execution-level map: a missing path or a non-array value expands
977	to zero instances and the map completes for that iteration with an empty
978	output list, so the loop boundary is evaluated as usual; an element count
979	beyond `max_instances` creates no instance at all — the map fails
980	permanently, is listed under `failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates
981	with reason `retries_exhausted` under the usual exhaustion semantics.
982	
983	The expanded instances belong to their iteration only: they queue in
984	ascending element index order and are settled one per `advance`, exactly
985	like execution-level instances, and one iteration's instances never
986	overwrite another iteration's results. An instance is an ordinary task in
987	every other respect — a submitted failure consumes the template's retry
988	bound and re-queues that instance within its iteration, and a template
989	approval point parks the execution until an approver decides it — with no
990	influence from the iteration number.
991	
992	Iteration state exposes each nested map under the iteration record's `maps`
993	field, with the same per-map shape as an execution-level map (`status`, one
994	record per instance, the ordered completed `outputs`, and `failure_reason`);
995	the field is present on every iteration of a loop whose body declares a map
996	node. When a nested map completes, its node enters the iteration's
997	`completed_nodes` and its output list is recorded in the iteration's
998	`outputs`; when the loop finishes, the usual roll-up lists the map node once
999	in the execution-level `completed_nodes`, while its outputs stay with their
1000	iterations. An execution-level `maps` field is not created for nested maps.
1001	
1002	Every event a nested expansion records carries the owning `loop_id` and
1003	`iteration` alongside the map id and, for per-instance events, the element
1004	`index`: `map_expanded`, `map_completed`, the per-instance `node_completed`,
1005	`node_failed`, and `node_retried`, and `approval_requested` and
1006	`approval_decided` for a template approval point. The `iteration_started`
1007	event of a loop whose body declares map nodes carries the iteration's
1008	initial `maps` skeleton, so replay rebuilds every iteration's instance list,
1009	status, and ownership solely from the event stream, consistent with the
1010	materialized state. Checkpoints are written at each iteration's instance
1011	boundaries, so recovery continues the current iteration's unfinished
1012	instances and never repeats an instance output. Cancellation, timeouts,
1013	leases, retries, and approvals keep their existing semantics, and a nested
1014	map never changes an execution's termination reason.
1015	
1016	Executions whose workflows declare no nested map behave exactly as before:
1017	state fields, event contents, and advancement results are unchanged.
1018	
1019	### Delete and modify expanded instances
1020	
1021	An expanded dynamic node offers, alongside expansion and per-instance
1022	advancement, two instance-level operations and a node-level re-expansion.
1023	All three are ordinary idempotent HTTP commands over the same entry points
1024	the rest of the service uses; they introduce no second protocol.
1025	
1026	An instance that has never advanced can be removed, and so can an instance
1027	that has permanently failed:
1028	
1029	```http
1030	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/2/delete
1031	Idempotency-Key: delete-instance-2
1032	
1033	{}
1034	```
1035	
1036	The body must be an empty object. Removing an instance drops only that
1037	instance's record: every retained instance keeps its element index, its
1038	place in the queue, and its advancement order. When the removed instance was
1039	the map's last unfinished instance, the node completes under the existing
1040	rules with an output list containing only the retained instances' outputs,
1041	in ascending element-index order, and its successors unlock as usual. An
1042	instance that is waiting on an approval, or has already completed, can never
1043	be deleted; attempting it returns `409 conflict` and changes no state. A
1044	permanently failed instance is removable after the execution has terminated,
1045	but removing it never revives the execution, alters its termination reason,
1046	or changes the node's failed conclusion. When every retained instance of a
1047	map inside a loop body has ended, the iteration's other nodes advance as
1048	usual and the node completes or ends under the existing rules; deleting an
1049	instance in one iteration never touches another iteration.
1050	
1051	An instance that has never advanced can also have its input rewritten
1052	before it is worked:
1053	
1054	```http
1055	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/1/modify
1056	Idempotency-Key: modify-instance-1
1057	
1058	{"input":{"address":"742 Evergreen Terrace"}}
1059	```
1060	
1061	The body must contain exactly `input`, an object with the new content; it is
1062	validated like every other request body (finite numbers only). The rewrite
1063	changes only the parameters used when that one instance is later advanced:
1064	it affects no other instance, and the output and history of an instance that
1065	has already advanced (waiting, completed, or permanently failed) are
1066	immutable — modifying such an instance returns `409 conflict` and changes no
1067	state. The rewritten input, including its full float precision and `-0.0`,
1068	is stored verbatim.
1069	
1070	Delete and modify calls on the same instance settle in call order: every
1071	call applies to the instance list exactly as the earlier calls left it, and
1072	several calls on one instance each take effect independently, one after
1073	another. A rewritten instance has still never advanced, so it remains
1074	deletable; deleting or modifying an instance an earlier call already
1075	removed is a `404 not_found`; and a second rewrite of the same instance
1076	records the first rewrite's content as its `before`.
1077	
1078	Both commands apply to a map nested in a loop body exactly as to an
1079	execution-level map: the current running iteration's instances are
1080	addressed by the same path, and every event they append carries the owning
1081	`loop_id` and `iteration` alongside the map id; an execution-level instance
1082	carries no loop context.
1083	
1084	An out-of-bounds element index, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic
1085	`map`, a missing execution, or a cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found`
1086	and writes nothing. A missing or mistyped field, a non-object modify
1087	`input`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a `400 validation_error`
1088	with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a
1089	`409 conflict`; repeating the same command with the same key returns the
1090	first result and appends no second event.
1091	
1092	Every successful call appends exactly one event to the execution stream:
1093	
1094	- an `instance_deleted` event records the action type, the owning dynamic
1095	  node under `map_id`, the removed instance's element `index` and `status`
1096	  (`ready` or `failed`), and, for a map inside a loop body, the `loop_id`
1097	  and `iteration`;
1098	- an `instance_modified` event records the action type, the owning
1099	  `map_id`, the instance `index`, the content `before` the rewrite (`null`
1100	  for an instance that had never been rewritten) and `after` it, and the
1101	  same loop context when the instance belongs to an iteration.
1102	
1103	Replay rebuilds the instance list, every instance's status and ownership,
1104	and each rewrite solely from the event stream: a delete drops the recorded
1105	instance (and the subsequent `map_completed`, when the deletion finished the
1106	node, completes it with the retained outputs), and a modify applies the
1107	rewritten input to that one instance, so the rebuilt state is exactly the
1108	materialized state. A checkpoint is written at the instance boundary of
1109	every successful delete or modify; after a restart recovery continues the
1110	unfinished instances, repeats no instance output, and never resurrects a
1111	deleted instance. The operations change no advancement conclusion or
1112	termination semantics: cancellation, timeouts, approvals, leases, retries,
1113	and retry exhaustion keep their existing behavior. Executions that never
1114	use deletion, modification, or re-expansion keep exactly their current
1115	state fields, event contents, and advancement results.
1116	
1117	### Re-expand a dynamic node
1118	
1119	A dynamic node that has already expanded can be expanded again on demand —
1120	above all to regenerate its instance list after deletions:
1121	
1122	```http
1123	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/reexpand
1124	Idempotency-Key: reexpand-1
1125	
1126	{}
1127	```
1128	
1129	(The same operation is also accepted at `.../maps/ship/expand`.) The body
1130	must be an empty object. Re-expansion reads the element list again from the
1131	source task's recorded output — the same recorded output the first
1132	expansion read, which never changes once recorded — and regenerates the
1133	instance list from it: every previous instance record is replaced, and the
1134	fresh instances queue from element index zero in ascending order. The
1135	regenerated instances are ordinary instances in every respect: they are
1136	deleted, modified, advanced, retried, and approved through the same entries
1137	and with exactly the same behavior as a first expansion, and their retry
1138	bounds start from zero.
1139	
1140	Every successful call appends exactly one `map_reexpanded` event, recording
1141	the action type, the owning dynamic node under `map_id`, and the number of
1142	generated instances under `instance_count`; for a map inside a loop body
1143	the event also carries the owning `loop_id` and `iteration`, and only the
1144	current running iteration's expansion is replaced. A node that had
1145	completed returns to `running`: it leaves `completed_nodes`, its recorded
1146	output entry is discarded, and when the regenerated instances have all
1147	completed the node completes again under the existing rules, its result
1148	list holding only the finally retained instances' outputs in ascending
1149	element-index order. An empty element list completes the node again at
1150	once with an empty output list, exactly like a zero-element first
1151	expansion.
1152	
1153	Re-expansion is rejected with `409 conflict` and writes nothing when the
1154	node has not expanded yet, when it has permanently failed, when one of its
1155	instances is waiting on an approval decision, when the execution has
1156	already completed, or when a nested map's loop is not currently running.
1157	A terminated execution's unfinished node may still be re-expanded; doing so
1158	never revives the execution or alters its termination reason. A missing
1159	execution, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic `map`, or a
1160	cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found` and writes nothing. A
1161	non-empty or non-object body, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
1162	`400 validation_error` with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key
1163	from another operation is a `409 conflict`; repeating the same call with
1164	the same key returns the first result and appends no second event. Replay
1165	rebuilds the regenerated instance list, statuses, and ownership solely
1166	from the event stream, a checkpoint is written at the re-expansion
1167	boundary, and recovery after a restart continues the unfinished
1168	regenerated instances — repeating no instance output and never resurrecting
1169	an instance that stayed deleted.
1170	
1171	### Workflow versions
1172	
1173	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
1174	
1175	```json
1176	{
1177	  "id": "order-flow",
1178	  "version": "2026-09-25",
1179	  "nodes": [
1180	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
1181	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
1182	  ]
1183	}
1184	```
1185	
1186	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
1187	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
1188	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
1189	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
1190	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
1191	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
1192	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
1193	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
1194	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
1195	
1196	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
1197	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
1198	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
1199	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
1200	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
1201	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
1202	
1203	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
1204	current version at the moment it starts:
1205	
1206	```http
1207	POST /executions
1208	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
1209	
1210	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
1211	```
1212	
1213	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
1214	
1215	```json
1216	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
1217	```
1218	
1219	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
1220	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
1221	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
1222	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
1223	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
1224	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
1225	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
1226	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
1227	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
1228	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
1229	conclusions never change.
1230	
1231	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
1232	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
1233	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
1234	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
1235	stream with no added field.
1236	
1237	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
1238	
1239	```http
1240	GET /workflows/order-flow
1241	```
1242	
1243	```json
1244	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
1245	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
1246	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
1247	]}
1248	```
1249	
1250	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
1251	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
1252	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
1253	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
1254	resources as usual.
1255	
1256	### Migrate a running execution to another version
1257	
1258	```http
1259	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
1260	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
1261	
1262	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
1263	```
1264	
1265	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
1266	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
1267	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
1268	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
1269	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
1270	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
1271	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
1272	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
1273	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
1274	carries the target version.
1275	
1276	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
1277	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
1278	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
1279	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
1280	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
1281	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
1282	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
1283	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
1284	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
1285	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
1286	
1287	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
1288	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
1289	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
1290	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
1291	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
1292	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
1293	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
1294	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
1295	content.
1296	
1297	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
1298	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
1299	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
1300	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
1301	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
1302	`400 validation_error`. Migrating a running execution to the version it is
1303	already bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and
1304	writing no checkpoint; a `completed` or `terminated` execution instead
1305	returns `409 conflict` even when the target version is exactly the one it is
1306	bound to. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
1307	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
1308	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
1309	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
1310	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.
1311	
1312	### Start an execution
1313	
1314	```http
1315	POST /executions
1316	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
1317	
1318	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
1319	```
1320	
1321	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
1322	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;
1323	naming a `version` binds to that one instead (and a missing version is a
1324	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.
1325	
1326	An execution may declare a timeout:
1327	
1328	```json
1329	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
1330	```
1331	
1332	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
1333	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
1334	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
1335	a timeout never expire.
1336	
1337	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
1338	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
1339	
1340	```json
1341	{
1342	  "id": "run-3",
1343	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
1344	  "input": {},
1345	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
1346	}
1347	```
1348	
1349	### List workflows
1350	
1351	```http
1352	GET /workflows?limit=50
1353	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1354	```
1355	
1356	Enumerates the workflows declared in the request's namespace. The response
1357	is `{"workflows":[{"id":"order-flow"}, ...]}`: one entry per workflow, each
1358	carrying its identifier, in ascending identifier order. A namespace with no
1359	workflows gets the definite empty result `{"workflows":[]}`, not an error.
1360	The query is read-only: it creates nothing, appends no events, and records
1361	no usage, so repeating it returns the same answer and changes no stored
1362	state.
1363	
1364	The list is paged with a keyset cursor:
1365	
1366	- `limit` — required; the maximum number of entries in the page, a positive
1367	  integer. The page never holds more entries than the limit;
1368	- `cursor` — optional; the identifier of the previous page's last entry.
1369	  Only entries whose identifier sorts strictly after the cursor are
1370	  returned, so paging with the previous page's last identifier yields
1371	  consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A cursor past the end
1372	  returns the definite empty list.
1373	
1374	### List executions
1375	
1376	```http
1377	GET /executions?workflow_id=order-flow&status=terminated&termination_reason=timeout&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=run-41&limit=50
1378	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1379	```
1380	
1381	Enumerates the executions in the request's namespace in ascending execution
1382	identifier order. The response is `{"executions":[...]}`; each entry carries
1383	the execution `id`, its `workflow_id`, its `status` (`running`, `completed`,
1384	or `terminated`, always a string), its `termination_reason` (one of the
1385	four termination reasons for a terminated execution, otherwise `null`), and
1386	its `created_at` (the ISO-8601 UTC creation timestamp ending in `Z`), in
1387	that stable key order. A namespace with no executions gets the definite
1388	empty result `{"executions":[]}`. Like the workflows list this query is
1389	read-only and never settles a due timeout, appends an event, writes a
1390	checkpoint, or records usage, so repeated calls return the same answer and
1391	change no state or metering conclusion.
1392	
1393	The same `limit` and `cursor` pagination applies, with the cursor taken
1394	from the previous page's last execution identifier. In addition, five
1395	filters may be combined, and every given filter must match:
1396	
1397	- `workflow_id` — only executions of that workflow. Referencing a workflow
